title: The Zoo
victoryHeadline: Caught! His story didn't hold water.
acts: It was the kind of Saturday the zoo ran on: crowded, sunny, and entirely too busy for anyone to be watching anyone else. Over by the Lion Habitat, Ivan had one eye on a lion that had drifted too close to the fence line and the other on a visitor who had somehow got past the rope entirely — Carolyn, crouched behind a shrub with her phone out, angling for the shot of her life. At the Crocodile pool, Gordon had set up a folding chair at the water's edge, the exact spot he came to every spring, and was already three-quarters asleep in the sun while Nancy waded in nearby after something a child on the viewing platform had dropped.

In the Main Area, a much smaller and much louder drama was under way. Flavia had claimed a chair an hour earlier and was now defending it, arms folded, from a threat that existed nowhere except in her own head. Deborah paced past with the map held upside down, narrating a complaint about the signage into a notebook she'd have denied carrying if asked. Alfred stood at the rail with headphones the size of dinner plates clamped over his ears, filming penguins and hearing precisely none of it. Out at the Shark tank, meanwhile, the afternoon feed rattled along the way it always did, one keeper flinging fish and the other shouting the count back across the water, both losing the argument to the wind. Whatever it was that happened at the far end of the park that afternoon — and something clearly did, because for one moment half the zoo's water pressure seemed to surge somewhere all at once with a sound like a slammed door underwater — nobody at the Main Area noticed, because Flavia had just raised her voice about the chair.

By the time the tannoy crackled for the second time, calm and a little too insistent, the smaller dramas had mostly sorted themselves out. Ivan had finally talked Carolyn back over the rope, photo secured, lion unbothered, and Flavia's chair sat empty and undisturbed, its imaginary threat having apparently lost interest and gone home. Over at the crocodile pool and the shark tank the ordinary business of a Saturday wound down without incident, as it did every week. Only when a keeper was sent to check the far enclosures did anyone learn that the loud noise nobody had investigated an hour earlier had not, in fact, been the water pressure acting up on its own.

whereabouts.A: Alfred was pressed against the Main Area rail with over-ear headphones clamped on, filming a family of penguins doing absolutely nothing remarkable and getting, by his own count, his best footage of the year.
whereabouts.B: Barry, moustache and dreadlocks, had cornered a spare visitor at his Concessions table and had no intention of letting her leave before she'd heard the full, unedited account of the eleven-pound bass he'd landed off Pier Seven three summers back.
whereabouts.C: Carolyn had slipped over the low rope into the Lion Habitat for one photograph from behind a shrub, phone held at arm's length, entirely unaware the lion had already clocked her and was, for once, too comfortable to bother caring.
whereabouts.D: Deborah paced the Main Area with the park map held upside down, drafting — in a notebook she'd never admit to carrying — her four hundred and twelfth review for a niche signage-rating blog with exactly nine subscribers, one of them her sister.
whereabouts.E: Eloise stood beside the Concessions table eating chips straight from the bag, on the grounds, stated twice already that day, that sitting down at a sticky table was a compromise she was not prepared to make.
whereabouts.F: Flavia had claimed a chair in the Main Area an hour earlier and was now defending it, arms folded, glasses down her nose, against a queue of precisely nobody who had shown the faintest interest in taking it.
whereabouts.G: Gordon had brought a folding chair from home and set it at the crocodile water's edge, the same spot he and his late wife used to sit every spring, and dozed off there in the afternoon sun without meaning to.
whereabouts.H: Henry spent the afternoon at the Entrance table restocking leaflets and working out, not for the first time, exactly how much a family ticket had gone up since he'd started the job.
whereabouts.I: Ivan spent twenty solid minutes coaxing a lion back from the fence line while simultaneously, and far less successfully, trying to persuade a visitor behind a shrub that the rope was there for a reason.
whereabouts.J: Jim spent the afternoon on hose duty at the Elephant Habitat, topping up the pool ahead of the four o'clock bath and trading the same tired complaint about water pressure with Vlad that the two of them seemed to have every single week.
whereabouts.K: Kaiden came off the shark feed with scales down one arm and something dark and unmistakably fish-shaped across her shirt, which alarmed exactly one passing visitor until she held up the bucket and the mystery solved itself.
whereabouts.L: Langston stood waist-deep in the penguin pool with a long-handled brush, scrubbing algae off the rockwork while every single penguin in the enclosure gathered on the dry side to supervise from a safe distance.
whereabouts.M: Mara stood in the second column of the shark pool shouting the feed count back across the water to Kaiden, losing at least four fish to the wind and insisting, as always, that every other one had landed exactly right.
whereabouts.N: Nancy waded into the crocodile pool to retrieve a sun hat a child had dropped from the viewing platform, and spent a happy minute working out how best to return it to a family she'd already lost in the crowd.
whereabouts.O: Oliver crouched behind a boulder in the Bear Habitat, doling out berries from a bucket to a bear who had, in fact, found the bucket four minutes earlier and was now simply enjoying the show.
whereabouts.V: Vlad did his usual end-of-day round of the Elephant Habitat, clipboard in hand, grumbling to Jim about the water pressure and making a note to chase maintenance about it again, first thing Monday.

reveal: It was Jim, in the Elephant Habitat, and the method was the very hose the two of them had just been arguing about. Maintenance had swapped in a wider valve to finally fix the pressure complaint, and that afternoon Jim tested it for the first time — with Vlad crouched at the pool's edge, sleeves rolled, checking the fitting himself at Jim's suggestion. Jim opened the valve knowing exactly what the new pressure would do at that range, and exactly where Vlad was kneeling to receive it. The rush of water caught him square in the side and sent him into the low poolside wall before he had time to make a sound. Jim shut the valve off just as calmly as he'd opened it, and told the first person who asked that he'd only been testing the fix Vlad himself had ordered.

escape.generic: The valve was written up as a maintenance fault, the pressure complaint got fixed for real this time, and somewhere in the park the real culprit is still filing the paperwork on it.

byAccused.A: Alfred was arrested with the footage still rolling, so the last thing on his camera is forty minutes of penguins and, right at the end, his own extremely surprised face — while the true culprit never made it into frame at all.
byAccused.B: Barry never got to finish the story about the eleven-pound bass, and to this day insists the arrest is the only thing that's kept it from getting any better — while the real killer went home to a quiet dinner.
byAccused.C: Carolyn's photograph from behind the shrub came out beautifully and made the local paper twice — once for the lion, and once, less happily, for her arrest a week later, by which point nobody was looking for anyone else.
byAccused.D: Deborah filed her four hundred and thirteenth signage review from a police station waiting room, gave the place two stars, and never learned the real culprit had walked straight past a sign she'd have rated rather highly.
byAccused.E: Eloise was still standing when they came for her — she'd never once sat down all day, she pointed out, which struck her as exactly the kind of detail an innocent person would have — and the real killer let her make the point uncontested.
byAccused.F: Flavia was hauled away from the chair she'd guarded for two hours, and her one request — that somebody keep an eye on it for her — went unmet, same as the actual investigation.
byAccused.G: Gordon was led off still folding up his chair, quietly glad, at least, that nobody made him leave it behind — while the real killer never had to explain a thing to anybody.
byAccused.H: Henry, alone at the Entrance all afternoon with nothing but leaflets for company, learned the hard way that having no witnesses cuts both directions — and the guilty party walked straight past his empty table.
byAccused.I: Ivan was pulled off lion duty mid-negotiation, and the lion, unbothered either way, went back to ignoring everybody equally, including whoever had actually done it.
byAccused.K: Kaiden was taken away still faintly smelling of the shark feed, which several officers mentioned and none of them found remotely funny — while the real killer, by comparison, smelled entirely innocent.
byAccused.L: Langston was hauled out of the penguin pool dripping and confused, and the penguins, for the first time all day, looked faintly sorry to see him go — small comfort, since the real killer got away perfectly dry.
byAccused.M: Mara's fish count came in four short that day and stayed that way permanently, a discrepancy nobody but her ever noticed or cared about — much like the actual culprit, who nobody noticed either.
byAccused.N: Nancy never did track down the family with the missing sun hat, and always wondered afterward whether they simply assumed she'd kept it — a much smaller injustice than the one actually taking place.
byAccused.O: Oliver was led away from his boulder still holding the berry bucket, and the bear, finally left alone with it, came out of the whole affair rather better than anyone else involved.
